meta.case_name: Refinery in the Country of Georgia

prompt.context: It is 2012 and your client is one of the largest retailers of oil products in the country of Georgia (Eastern Europe). The company is exploring the idea to build a crude oil refinery in Georgia and has hired you to evaluate the idea. The goal of the company is to understand what the capacity of the refinery should be and to make a go/no-go decision.
prompt.question: What should the refinery's capacity be, and should the client proceed with building a crude oil refinery in Georgia?

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's current market share?
clarifying_info.a: The company controls roughly 25% of all oil product sales in Georgia.

clarifying_info.q: Are there existing refineries in Georgia?
clarifying_info.a: Currently there are no crude refineries in Georgia. All refined oil products are imported from other countries.

clarifying_info.q: What oil products should we consider?
clarifying_info.a: For simplicity, consider three major oil products: Gasoline, Diesel, and Other Oil Products.

clarifying_info.q: How much crude oil does Georgia produce?
clarifying_info.a: Georgia produces 100,000 tons of crude oil annually and this number is projected to stay stable. All crude is currently exported to foreign countries.
The possibility of importing crude oil from neighboring countries is limited. Importing from countries further away is associated with high transportation costs.
An oil refinery is a plant where the input is crude oil and the output is final products ready for retail consumption, like gasoline, diesel, etc.

exhibits.title: Crude Oil Production and Oil Products Consumption in Georgia
exhibits.shows: A table of Georgia's annual crude oil production (2010-2014, with 2013-2014 projected) and a table of oil products consumption in Georgia by product type (Diesel, Gasoline, Other Products) for 2012 and 2013. Also includes two industry fact bullets about transportation costs and pricing.

exhibits.title: Expected Output from Georgian Crude Oil and Wholesale Prices
exhibits.shows: A pie chart showing the percentage breakdown of outputs from Georgian crude oil (Gasoline 30%, Diesel 50%, Other Oil Products 15%, Loss 5%), and a table of wholesale prices of oil products in Georgia.

framework: Identify this as an investment/go-no-go case requiring both quantitative and qualitative analysis
Quantitative: Determine refinery capacity based on available crude supply and local demand; then build financial projections (revenue, costs, NPV)
Revenue: Estimate output product mix from crude, apply wholesale prices to get total revenue
Costs: Break into CapEx (construction), fixed costs (labor, overheads), and variable costs (crude oil purchase)
NPV: Use DCF — perpetuity formula NPV = EBIT(1-t) / discount rate minus initial investment
Qualitative: Assess availability of raw materials, local demand, price risk, competition, and other risks before final recommendation

questions.prompt: What should the refinery's capacity be?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Exhibit 1 to identify that Georgia produces ~100,000 tons of crude oil per year (stable projection), all of which is currently exported. There is no meaningful ability to import additional crude. Therefore the maximum feasible capacity is ~100,000 tons. Candidate should also note that 100,000 tons is roughly 10% of total local consumption (~890,000 tons in 2012), and that high transportation costs mean local production would be price-competitive, ensuring sufficient demand.

math.setup: Total Georgia crude production ≈ 100,000 tons/year (stable). Total oil products consumed in Georgia 2012 = 380,000 + 470,000 + 40,000 = 890,000 tons. Refinery output of 100,000 tons represents ~11% of local consumption.
steps: Capacity = 100,000 tons (limited by available crude supply)
math.answer: Refinery capacity should be ~100,000 tons, constrained by domestic crude supply.

questions.prompt: Calculate the capital expenditure (CapEx) for the refinery.
questions.guidance: Candidate should take the capacity (100,000 tons) and apply the construction cost rate. The client already owns the land so it can be ignored.

math.setup: CapEx = capacity in 1,000-ton units × cost per 1,000 tons

questions.prompt: Calculate the fixed costs (labor and overhead).
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm fixed vs. variable costs. Labor is driven by capacity; overheads are a percentage of revenue. Overhead requires revenue to be calculated first (or flagged as a dependency).

math.setup: Labor: 1 employee per 1,000 tons of capacity × $20,000/year. Overheads: 10% of total revenue ($85,500,000).
math.answer: Labor: $2,000,000; Other overheads: $8,550,000; Total fixed costs: $10,550,000

questions.guidance: Candidate should identify two variables: output volumes by product and price per product. From 100,000 tons of crude, apply the percentage breakdown from Exhibit 2 to get tons of each product, then multiply by wholesale price.

math.setup: Output tons by product = 100,000 × product percentage. Revenue = output tons × price per ton.

questions.guidance: The variable cost is the purchase price of crude oil — 100,000 tons at $600/ton.

math.setup: Variable cost = crude oil volume × market price per ton

questions.prompt: Calculate NPV of the project. Client wants to use a DCF model — assume Year 1 projections remain constant in perpetuity with no growth. Discount rate: 10%. Tax rate: 20%. Ignore depreciation.
questions.guidance: Candidate should use perpetuity formula: NPV = EBIT(1-t) / discount rate − initial investment. Walk through: total revenue minus total costs = EBIT, apply tax, divide by discount rate, subtract CapEx.

math.setup: NPV = [EBIT × (1 − tax rate)] / discount rate − CapEx

brainstorming.prompt: The NPV looks attractive. What risks, weaknesses in assumptions, or qualitative factors should the client consider before making a final go/no-go decision?

categories.name: Raw Material Supply Risk
ideas: Domestic crude production could decline, reducing refinery throughput
Limited ability to import crude from neighbors constrains upside and creates a single-source dependency
Crude oil market price volatility directly impacts variable costs ($600/ton assumption may not hold)

categories.name: Demand and Pricing Risk
ideas: Wholesale price assumptions ($900-$1,000/ton) could fall if global oil prices drop
Local demand growth assumptions may not materialize
Client controls only 25% of retail market — other 75% may not purchase from the refinery

categories.name: Operational and Execution Risk
ideas: Construction cost overruns could increase CapEx beyond $50M
Refinery operations require specialized expertise not currently held by a retailer
Environmental permits and regulatory approvals may delay or block construction

categories.name: Competitive and Market Structure Risk
ideas: Currently 100% of oil products are imported — existing import relationships/contracts may resist disruption
New entrants could also build refineries, increasing competition
Political risk in Georgia (Eastern Europe) could affect operations or profitability

categories.name: Financial Model Assumptions
ideas: Perpetuity assumption with no growth is simplistic — demand may grow or shrink
Ignoring depreciation understates true economic cost
No account for working capital needs or maintenance CapEx
10% discount rate may understate risk for a capital project in an emerging market

categories.name: Strategic Fit
ideas: Building a refinery is a very different business from oil product retailing
Management bandwidth and capability to operate industrial infrastructure
Potential to sell crude oil throughput to competitors if refinery has excess capacity

recommendation: Proceed with building a 100,000-ton crude oil refinery in Georgia
The project generates a positive NPV of approximately $69.6 million, representing strong value creation relative to the $50 million investment
The refinery would process all domestically produced crude (currently exported at low prices) and supply ~11% of local demand that currently relies entirely on expensive imports
risks: Crude oil price volatility could significantly compress margins given crude is ~70% of total costs
The perpetuity/no-growth model is optimistic — any demand or price deterioration erodes the NPV cushion
Operational risk is high: the client has no experience running industrial refinery operations
Limited crude supply upside: capacity is capped at ~100,000 tons with no import alternative
next_steps: Conduct detailed feasibility study including site selection, permitting, and engineering cost estimates
Develop a crude oil supply agreement with domestic producers to secure feedstock
Model sensitivity analysis on crude oil price and refined product price assumptions
Assess management capability gap and identify whether to hire refinery operators or partner with an experienced operator
Explore off-take agreements with other retailers to ensure the full 100,000-ton output can be sold
